items.stem: Why is risk adjustment applied before comparing hospital outcome rates?

options.text: Hospitals treat different patient mixes, so raw rates are not comparable
options.rationale: Correct: risk adjustment accounts for differing patient severity.

options.text: It makes all hospitals look the same
options.rationale: It controls for case mix, not to equalise results artificially.

options.text: It is only a billing requirement
options.rationale: It is an analytic necessity for fair comparison.

items.explanation: Correct: risk adjustment accounts for differing patient severity.

items.stem: Which TWO are required to responsibly de-identify a patient dataset? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Remove or generalise identifiers beyond just the name, including dates and small geographies
options.rationale: Correct: many quasi-identifiers can re-identify a person.

options.text: Limit the data to the minimum necessary for the purpose
Keep full dates of birth because they are not names
options.rationale: Full dates are strong quasi-identifiers and must be handled.

options.text: Share the raw record widely to speed analysis
options.rationale: Wide sharing of raw records violates privacy principles.

items.explanation: Correct: many quasi-identifiers can re-identify a person.

items.stem: An observational analysis shows patients on a drug had better outcomes. What is the safest interpretation?

options.text: The association may be confounded; it does not prove the drug caused the outcome
options.rationale: Correct: observational associations can be driven by confounders.

options.text: The drug definitely caused the better outcomes
options.rationale: Observational data cannot establish causation on its own.
That contradicts the observed association and is unsupported.

options.text: No further analysis is ever needed
options.rationale: Confounding must be investigated before any causal claim.

items.explanation: Correct: observational associations can be driven by confounders.
